dimensions.name: Understanding the skeleton, decode/runtime contract, and spec-test harness

evidence.note: Enumerated all src files, listed the simd spec dir, and read ~5 source files (decode.rs, runtime.rs, types.rs, spec.rs, main.rs) up front before editing — establishing the skeleton's structure.
Built, ran i32.json/block.json spec tests and the full suite, then grepped FAIL output to locate which MVP assertions were failing — grounding work in the harness output format.
Inspected wabt's opcode.h/opcode.def to cross-check the 0xFD SIMD sub-opcode space against the real WASM SIMD encoding before generating decode/exec tables — a strong level-8 orientation element.

Identified the concrete unimplemented/buggy functions (Call, CallIndirect, exec_numeric, Return draining bug, exec_load sign-extension, v128 lane accessor stubs) and inspected NumOp/SimdOp enums — accurate model of dispatch and the locked contract.
Grepped for Call/CallIndirect/Return/exec_numeric/exec_load/v128_get/v128_set/exec_one and re-read the SimdOp enum, mapping the value-stack dispatch structure it needed to slot SIMD into.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly cleared the level-5 bar: it read decode.rs/runtime.rs/types.rs/spec.rs, located value types and dispatch, identified every buggy/unimplemented function, and used the spec-test harness output. It reached into level 8 by cross-checking the 0xFD sub-opcode families against wabt's real encoding tables and inspecting the NumOp/SimdOp enums. It falls short of 8-10 because there is no clear evidence it inspected the actual spec JSON assertion structure (only ran the harness), it never explicitly enumerated the public items locked by spec.rs/main.rs, and it did not proactively surface the tricky semantic contracts (NaN canonicalization, saturation, laneidx/memarg layout) before coding. That places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 7.

dimensions.name: Sequencing the fix + the SIMD opcode families into checkable milestones

evidence.note: Explicit two-phase ordering with rationale: 'fix all MVP bugs first, then implement SIMD' / 'fix MVP bugs first, then build SIMD incrementally' — separates the MVP-fix phase from SIMD, part of anchor 5.

MVP phase decomposed into a concrete ordered punch list (Return, Call, CallIndirect, exec_numeric, sign-extension loads), and step 157 lays out fix-load → fix-Return → Call/CallIndirect → exec_numeric → V128 accessors → Simd dispatch → exec_simd, showing dependency-respecting ordering.
Identifies a v128-plumbing foundation (SimdOp enum, 0xFD decode, lane accessor helpers, expect_v128) as a distinct layer before execution — a partial front-loading of shared infrastructure.

SIMD is planned as one undifferentiated block ('implement all ~200 SIMD opcodes' via generator), never broken into the named families (bitwise/int/float/saturating/widen-narrow/conversions/dot/q15) as milestones, and never tied to specific spec_json/simd/*.json files as done-signals.
Only three SetTodoList calls total; the milestone list is not kept live across the long patching struggle and shows no per-family SIMD tracking.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly separates the MVP-fix phase from SIMD with explicit ordering rationale, decomposes the MVP bugs into a concrete list, and identifies a v128 plumbing layer as a foundation before execution — placing it above anchor 3. However, it never lists the SIMD arithmetic families as sub-goals nor maps any family to its spec_json/simd/*.json file as a completion check; SIMD (the bulk and hard part) is treated as one monolithic generated block. That missing family-level, spec-file-gated milestone structure is the heart of this dimension, holding it below anchor 5 at a 4.

dimensions.name: Driving development with per-file spec tests and the full-suite score

evidence.note: Ran individual per-family spec files (i32.json, block.json) plus the full run_tests.py suite and read /tmp/score.txt to establish a baseline — genuine oracle use, above the 'only cargo build' anchor.
Grepped FAIL lines on i32.json and block.json to diagnose specific broken assertions — isolates individual family files and reads failures (above anchor 3).
Periodic full-suite runs during work, consistent with anchor-5 'full suite periodically'.

The bulk of the trajectory is a compile-fix struggle (restore/patch/regenerate runtime.rs). No SIMD family spec JSON is ever run; the agent never reaches a compiling SIMD build, so the per-family implement→test→fix loop for SIMD never materializes.
Trajectory ends mid-implementation (delegating runtime generation) with no SIMD spec test ever executed — the tight loop of anchor 8 and the subtle-case checks of anchor 10 are absent.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent used the spec-test oracle correctly for the MVP baseline: running individual family files (i32, block), reading FAIL lines to localize failures, and running the full suite periodically — clearly above anchor 3 and touching anchor-5 behavior. However, across the whole horizon it never sustained a per-family implement→run-specific-JSON→fix→rerun loop for any SIMD family, because it stalled in a long compile struggle and the run ends before any SIMD test is executed, and there is no evidence of verification designed for subtle NaN/saturation/rounding cases (anchors 8/10). This lands between anchors 3 and 5, at a 4.

dimensions.name: Tracking pass-rate and done-vs-remaining across the opcode surface

evidence.note: Established an early baseline by running per-file spec tests and the full run_tests.py score — but this was the last real aggregate measurement of the run.
Ran run_tests.py once more, still before any SIMD code compiled; the score was never re-checked or compared over time as edits proceeded thereafter.
Agent had to grep to rediscover that 'Return and Call are already patched!' — direct evidence it lost track of the current file/work state.
runtime.rs.bak restored and re-patched 14+ times with recurring angle-bracket corruption; the circular thrashing was never recognized as a stall, and no per-file pass/fail ledger was maintained.
A few SetTodoList/TaskList checklists were created but not maintained; a system-reminder flags the todo list as stale, showing the checklist was not kept current.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent measured the score only at the start (steps 7, 49) and never compared it over time, and it demonstrably lost track of what was already implemented (rediscovering patches at steps 110-114) while thrashing through 14+ restore/re-patch cycles it never recognized as circular — matching anchor 3's 'vague recollection of progress, re-debugs working code, score checked rarely and not compared.' A few family checklists nudge toward 5, but they were abandoned and no running pass-rate ledger existed, so the dominant behavior sits at 3.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when spec failures reveal wrong assumptions

evidence.note: Ran MVP spec tests (i32, block) and grepped FAIL output early, showing some test-failure awareness, but no explicit hypothesis-forming from the assertion detail.

Investigated wabt opcode.h/opcode.def to establish correct SIMD sub-opcode encoding proactively — avoids a wrong-encoding assumption, but this is pre-emptive verification rather than correction after a contradicting failure.

Identified pre-existing MVP bugs (Return draining all values, Call/CallIndirect unimplemented, load sign-extension) chiefly by reading code rather than diagnosing from failing MVP assertions; fixes match part of anchor 5.

Repeatedly restored runtime.rs from backup (~15 times) after the same Python code-generation approach corrupted angle brackets — course-correction of its own tooling, but re-applying a non-working method many times before switching; tangential to spec-failure-driven model revision.
Trajectory ends with exec_simd still a stub; the agent never ran SIMD spec tests, so no correction of wrong SIMD semantic assumptions (NaN, lane order, saturation, trunc_sat) was ever observed.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows partial anchor-5 behavior — it reacts to MVP tests and corrects identified MVP bugs — but most bug diagnosis comes from code reading rather than from failing-assertion detail, and there is no evidence of root-cause updates to a wrong SIMD semantic/encoding model because the trajectory ends before any SIMD test is run. The bulk of the horizon is spent thrashing on its own tooling (repeatedly restoring after the same corrupting generator approach), which is low-quality course-correction and tangential to spec-revealed wrong assumptions. This lands between anchor 3 (superficial reaction / repeating non-working approach) and anchor 5 (hypothesis-forming and MVP-bug correction), so a 4.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon systems task: fix an existing partial WebAssembly interpreter (bugs + unimplemented functions) and then implement the entire SIMD 128-bit proposal — hundreds of opcodes across ~10 instruction families, a new v128 value type, and many subtle semantics (lane shapes, saturation, NaN handling, signed/unsigned, rounding). Difficulty comes from breadth (hundreds of ops), depth (bit-exact IEEE/saturation correctness), a hard constraint (do not touch spec.rs/main.rs, keep public signatures), and a demanding bar (score must equal exactly 1.0). Spec-test JSON files give a precise, per-assertion oracle, so meta-work is heavily rewarded: orienting to the skeleton, sequencing families, and running spec tests incrementally are the difference between steady convergence and thrash across a huge opcode surface.

dimensions.name: Understanding the skeleton, decode/runtime contract, and spec-test harness
dimensions.description: Reading the existing interpreter (decode.rs, runtime.rs, types.rs, spec.rs) to learn the value-stack model, dispatch structure, and public items that must be preserved, and understanding how spec_json tests encode assertions before writing SIMD code.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task forbids rewriting and pins public signatures; SIMD support must slot into the existing value type / dispatch machinery. Guessing opcode encodings or value representation without reading the skeleton and a sample spec JSON leads to pervasive rework across hundreds of ops.

anchors.0: Starts editing or adding SIMD handlers without reading the existing source or any spec JSON; unaware which items spec.rs/main.rs import.
anchors.3: Skims one or two files; runs a build; has a vague idea of the value stack but never inspects the decode dispatch or a spec-test JSON structure.
anchors.5: Reads decode.rs/runtime.rs/types.rs enough to locate where value types and opcode dispatch live, identifies the unimplemented/buggy functions, and inspects at least one spec JSON to understand assertion format before coding.
anchors.8: Builds an accurate mental model: how values flow on the stack, how memarg/LEB128 decoding works, exactly which public items are locked by spec.rs/main.rs, how v128 must integrate with the existing Value enum, and how the 0xFD u32 sub-opcode space maps to instruction families — cross-checked against a real spec JSON and the WASM SIMD encoding.
anchors.10: All of the above, plus proactively surfacing the genuinely tricky contracts before they bite (NaN canonicalization in assert_return, signed/unsigned lane semantics, saturation vs wrapping, load_lane memarg+laneidx encoding), and using the existing MVP opcode handlers as a template so SIMD code matches house style and reuses helpers rather than reinventing them.

dimensions.name: Sequencing the fix + the SIMD opcode families into checkable milestones
dimensions.description: Breaking the work into an ordered plan — first make MVP tests green (fix bugs/unimplemented funcs), then add v128 plumbing, then implement SIMD families (const/splat/lanes, bitwise, int arith, float arith, saturating, widen/narrow, conversions, dot/q15, loads/stores) — each tied to specific spec JSON files as done-signals.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With hundreds of opcodes and a 1.0 bar, treating this as one undifferentiated push guarantees losing track of what's done. A family-by-family order, each gated on its spec file passing, converts an overwhelming surface into a sequence of verifiable wins.

anchors.0: No decomposition; implements opcodes in arbitrary order with no notion of milestones or which spec files gate which work.
anchors.3: A flat, generic todo like 'implement SIMD' with maybe two coarse buckets; no mapping to spec test files; no explicit ordering rationale.
anchors.5: Separates the MVP-fix phase from SIMD, and lists the SIMD families as sub-goals; roughly maps families to their spec JSON files as completion checks.
anchors.8: A clear ordered hierarchy: MVP green first, then v128 type + const/splat/lane extract-replace as the foundation, then dependent families in a sensible order (bitwise → int arith → float → saturating → widen/narrow → conversions → loads/stores → dot/q15), each milestone bound to its specific spec_json/simd/*.json file as the done-signal, with dependencies respected (e.g. lane ops before shuffle).
anchors.10: That ordering plus deliberate sequencing that front-loads shared infrastructure (a v128 representation + lane-extraction/reconstruction helpers) so later families collapse to thin wrappers, prioritizes families by assertion count / risk, and keeps the milestone list live and accurate as scope is discovered, so 'done vs remaining' is always legible across the full opcode surface.

dimensions.name: Driving development with per-file spec tests and the full-suite score
dimensions.description: Deliberately using the provided spec-test oracle: running individual spec JSON files per family during development and the aggregate run_tests.py score for overall progress, rather than assuming correctness or only checking at the end.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task ships a precise per-assertion oracle and demands exactly 1.0. An agent that leverages per-file tests as a tight feedback loop converges; one that only builds and eyeballs, or runs the whole suite blindly, cannot localize which of hundreds of ops is wrong.

anchors.0: Never runs spec tests (or only `cargo build`); declares completion without executing the oracle.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally but never isolates individual family JSON files; treats a low pass rate as one opaque number with no per-assertion diagnosis.
anchors.5: Runs the relevant per-family spec JSON after implementing each family and the full suite periodically; reads FAIL lines to find broken assertions.
anchors.8: Tight, deliberate loop: implement a family → run its specific spec JSON → read the exact failing assertion (line N, expected vs got) → fix → re-run, and uses the aggregate score to confirm no regressions in already-green files before moving on.
anchors.10: All that, plus verification designed for the subtle cases: deliberately checks NaN/canonical-NaN assertions, saturation boundary lanes, signed vs unsigned extract, and rounding modes; distinguishes a genuine semantic bug from a decode/encoding bug by narrowing to minimal failing cases; treats 'passes now' skeptically and confirms every previously-passing file still passes, driving toward a fully-earned 1.0 rather than a plateau.

dimensions.name: Tracking pass-rate and done-vs-remaining across the opcode surface
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which families/files pass, which remain, and whether recent edits raised or lowered the aggregate score, over a very long horizon.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Hundreds of opcodes and many spec files mean it is easy to lose the plot, re-touch already-correct code, or forget an entire family. An accurate running ledger tied to the score keeps the agent converging monotonically toward 1.0.

anchors.0: No sense of overall progress; cannot say which families are done or what the current pass rate is.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of progress; occasionally re-implements or re-debugs something already working; score checked rarely and not compared over time.
anchors.5: Keeps a usable checklist of families and roughly tracks the pass rate as work proceeds, noticing which spec files are green.
anchors.8: Maintains a precise, updated ledger of per-file pass/fail and the aggregate score trend, notices immediately when an edit drops previously-passing assertions (regression), and detects stalls where a family's failures aren't decreasing.
anchors.10: Sustained, self-aware monitoring across the whole horizon: always knows exact done-vs-remaining and current score, catches circular/thrashing debugging early (same file failing repeatedly), and reallocates effort toward the highest-assertion-count gaps to close the last distance to 1.0 efficiently rather than polishing already-green areas.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when spec failures reveal wrong assumptions
dimensions.description: When a spec test contradicts an assumed encoding or semantic (e.g. NaN handling, lane order, saturation, memarg/laneidx layout, or a pre-existing MVP bug), changing the model/implementation rather than repeating the same failing fix.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The interpreter already contains bugs, and SIMD has many counter-intuitive semantics; the constraint against rewriting means fixes must be surgical. Barrelling ahead on a falsified assumption about encoding or float semantics wastes the horizon and blocks 1.0.

anchors.0: Ignores contradicting test failures or keeps re-applying the same non-working change; never revisits an assumption.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures with superficial tweaks (guessing constants) without diagnosing the underlying wrong model; sometimes abandons a family when stuck.
anchors.5: When a family's tests fail, forms a hypothesis about the cause (wrong lane order, sign handling, encoding) and adjusts; corrects the identified MVP bugs based on failing MVP assertions.
anchors.8: Diagnoses root causes from the failing assertion detail and updates the mental model accordingly — e.g. realizing extract_lane_s must sign-extend, that trunc_sat clamps to lane bounds, or that canonical NaN comparison is required — then generalizes the fix across the affected family.
anchors.10: Systematic course-correction over the long horizon: recognizes when a wrong shared assumption (v128 byte order, LEB128 sub-opcode parsing, memory-endianness) is causing failures across many families and fixes it at the root, revises the plan/sequencing when a family proves harder than expected, and confirms the correction resolved the whole class of failures rather than one instance — without regressing prior work.
